help.d_projects: Every folder you work in. Add one with Add folder, start one from a template with New project, or try the demo project. Set a project On hold or Archive in its Setup tab; focus mode suggests which ones to put aside.
help.d_sessions: Every Claude Code, Codex and Gemini session is read from their own files: summary, health (tired, context full), what changed. Open one to read it, resume it, or replay it step by step.
help.d_chat: New chat starts Claude in a project, as yourself or as an expert. Plan mode plans before changing anything; approvals show as buttons. The prompt coach suggests what to add.
help.d_terminals: Real terminals in the browser, in any project, with Claude, Codex, Gemini or a plain shell.
help.d_memory: What Igrek learned about a project: decisions, conventions, failed approaches, open problems. AI sessions read it when they start. Export decisions as ADRs from the Memory tab.
help.d_inbox: Everything waiting for you: approvals, chats and terminals asking something, team runs, sites down, errors, expiring certificates, keys to change.
help.d_limits: How much of each AI plan is used, per account and expert. Accounts never switch by themselves; when the limit is full, team runs wait and go on after the reset.
help.d_personas: Experts with their own rules and notebooks (architect, backend, security, PM and more). Chat with one, hold a meeting, see their scores, or let two models compete in the model arena.
help.d_board: A project's board: moving a card to Doing starts the expert team in its own copy of the project; you approve before anything is merged. Roadmap shows milestones, sprints and a timeline; Import brings cards from Trello, Jira, Linear, Notion or GitHub.
help.d_schedules: Say it in a sentence ("every night check dependencies"); it runs on time in its own copy and waits for your approval.
help.d_preview: The app running in a panel: click an element, say what to change, see it change in seconds.
help.d_sections: Each project scored by category (security, tests, performance…), with what to fix first and a reviewer expert per category.
help.d_library: Books and documents experts cite, the lessons book of mistakes not to repeat, and the news of each expert's field.
help.d_servers: Your servers over SSH: health, files, commands with approval. A project's Environments tab deploys to staging or production with checks, a database backup first, staging copies and preview deploys of another branch.
help.d_tools: Uptime, domains and certificates, Docker, logs, databases, backups, calendar, the secret vault, costs, time spent and plugins: everything for running your projects without another app.
help.d_monitoring: A project's Monitoring tab: product numbers, user feedback, response times, errors from your app, logs, and incident mode with an automatic postmortem.
help.d_docs: Wiki pages with diagrams and [[links]], and whiteboards the AI reads as boxes and arrows. Write release notes, launch materials or a docs site from there.
help.d_github: Issues, pull requests and CI of a project, with your own gh login. Give an issue to the team in one click, or review a pull request in the app.
help.d_team: Share projects with your team, end-to-end encrypted: sessions, memory, wiki, comments, chat channels, and a board of who worked on what.
help.d_briefing: Morning briefing (yesterday, today, stuck), the evening recap of what we did, the end-of-day note for the team, and the weekly CEO report.
help.d_files: Browse and edit files of your projects; deletes go to a trash folder. Keys and secret folders are never opened.
help.d_prompts: Your prompt library, the prompt enhancer for lazy prompts, and your own shorthands.
help.d_ideas: Capture an idea from anywhere with Ctrl+I (or by voice); the CEO expert can review them.
help.d_settings: Language, theme, a free local model through Ollama, your own MCP servers, notifications to Telegram, Discord or e-mail, backups, updates, disk and network.
help.d_cli: igrek status, projects, search, ask, inbox, run, recap, weekly, and igrek api for any endpoint: everything from a script.
help.d_safety: Igrek never pushes or deploys by itself, never reads keys or .env values into AI, sends no telemetry (Settings > Network shows every address it opened), and the Stop all button (red while something runs) halts everything at once.

prompts.bodyHint: Use {name} for blanks you fill in each time, e.g. {file} or {feature}.
prompts.libraryHint: Well-tested prompts for the jobs people ask for most. Use one as it is, or add it to your list and make it your own.

prompts.startHint: A new chat opens with this prompt in the box. Nothing is sent until you press send.
prompts.emptyMine: You have not saved any prompts yet. Start from a ready-made one below, or write your own.
prompts.lib_code_review_body: Review the uncommitted changes in this project like a senior engineer. List problems by importance: bugs and broken behavior first, then security, then readability. For each one give the file and line, why it matters, and the fix. Do not change any code yet.
prompts.lib_pr_summary_body: Summarize the changes on this branch for a pull request: what changed and why, how to test it, risks and anything a reviewer should look at first. Plain words, short bullet points.
prompts.lib_bug_hunt_body: This is broken: {problem}. Find the cause before changing anything: reproduce it, read the related code, and tell me the root cause with the file and line. Then propose the smallest fix and a test that would have caught it.
prompts.lib_error_explain_body:
Explain this error in plain words, find where it comes from in this project, and fix it:

{error}
prompts.lib_tests_write_body: Write tests for {file}. Cover the normal cases, the edges (empty, one, many, invalid input) and the error paths. Use the project's existing test style and tools, run them, and show me the result.
prompts.lib_tests_missing_body: Find the most important code in this project that has no tests: what would hurt most if it broke. List the top five with the reason, then write tests for the first one.
prompts.lib_refactor_safe_body: Refactor {file} so it is easier to read and change, without changing what it does. First make sure tests cover it (write them if not), then change it in small steps and run the tests after each one.
prompts.lib_simplify_body: Look for code in this project that is more complicated than it needs to be: duplicate logic, dead code, abstractions used once. List what you would remove or merge and why. Change nothing until I agree.
prompts.lib_readme_body: Write or update the README of this project for someone new: what it is, why it exists, how to install and run it, how to use it, configuration, and where to get help. Check every command you write actually works.
prompts.lib_explain_project_body: Explain this project to me as if I just joined: what it does, how it is organized (the main folders and what lives where), how data flows through it, and the three files I should read first.
prompts.lib_security_review_body: Review this project for security problems, using the OWASP Top 10 as a guide: access control on every object, injection, authentication and sessions, secrets in code, risky dependencies. Rank findings by impact with the file, line and fix. Change nothing.
prompts.lib_secrets_check_body: Check this project for secrets that should not be there: keys, tokens and passwords in code, config files, logs or the git history. Do not print the secret values; tell me where they are and how to rotate and remove them.
prompts.lib_perf_check_body: {page} is slow. Measure before changing anything: find where the time goes (queries, network, rendering, loops), show me the numbers, then propose fixes ranked by how much time each saves.
prompts.lib_slow_query_body: This query or page is slow: {query}. Show its query plan, explain what the database is doing, and suggest indexes or a rewrite. Tell me what each change costs on writes.
prompts.lib_plan_feature_body: I want to add: {feature}. Before writing code, give me a short plan: what changes where (files and parts), the risky parts, open questions for me, and the steps in order. Wait for my approval.
prompts.lib_break_down_body: Split this into small tasks that can each be finished and tested in under a day: {task}. For each, write what done means. Put the riskiest one first.

readme.title: README at the top of the project
readme.fix: Add a README.md at the project root that says what the project is and how to run it.

bigFiles.title: Very long files: {{metric}}
bigFiles.fix: Split the longest files (over 600 lines) into smaller modules with one clear job each, without changing behaviour.

todo.title: TODO / FIXME notes: {{metric}}
todo.fix: Go through the TODO and FIXME comments: do the quick ones, turn the rest into tracked tasks, and remove stale ones.

types.title: Typed code: {{metric}}
types.fix: Convert the remaining JavaScript files to TypeScript, starting with the most used ones.

lint.title: Linter / formatter set up
lint.fix: Set up a linter and formatter (for example Biome or ESLint + Prettier, or Ruff for Python) with a config file in the repo.

strict.title: TypeScript strict mode
strict.fix: Turn on "strict": true in tsconfig.json and fix the type errors it reveals.

bigComponents.title: Very large UI components: {{metric}}
bigComponents.fix: Break the largest UI components (over 400 lines) into smaller components and hooks, keeping the UI identical.

any.title: Uses of "any": {{metric}}
any.fix: Replace "any" types with real types (or "unknown" plus a check) in the listed places.

errorBoundary.title: Error screen instead of a blank page
errorBoundary.fix: Add an error boundary (or the router's errorElement) so a crash shows a friendly error screen instead of a blank page.

i18n.title: Ready for other languages
i18n.fix: Move the UI texts into translation files with an i18n library so the app can be translated.

dark.title: Dark mode
dark.fix: Add a dark theme that follows the system setting (prefers-color-scheme) using shared color variables.

responsive.title: Works on small screens
responsive.fix: Make the layout responsive with breakpoints so it works on phones and narrow windows.

alt.title: Images without alt text: {{metric}}
alt.fix: Add meaningful alt text to the listed images (alt="" for purely decorative ones).

focus.title: Visible keyboard focus
focus.fix: Add clear :focus-visible styles so keyboard users can see where they are.

validation.title: Input validation
validation.fix: Validate request bodies and parameters with a schema library (for example zod or valibot; pydantic in Python) at the API boundary.

rateLimit.title: Rate limiting
rateLimit.fix: Add rate limiting to login and other expensive or public endpoints.

emptyCatch.title: Errors silently swallowed: {{metric}}
emptyCatch.fix: In the listed places, handle or log the error instead of ignoring it with an empty catch.

migrations.title: Database migrations
migrations.fix: Manage schema changes with versioned migrations instead of changing tables by hand.

injection.title: Queries built from strings: {{metric}}
injection.fix: In the listed queries, pass values as bound parameters instead of inserting them with ${...} (SQL injection risk).

ci.title: Automatic checks on every push (CI)
ci.fix: Add a CI workflow (for example GitHub Actions) that installs, lints, type-checks and runs the tests on every push.

dockerUser.title: Containers don't run as root
dockerUser.fix: Add a non-root USER to the listed Dockerfiles.

dockerignore.title: .dockerignore present
dockerignore.fix: Add a .dockerignore that leaves out node_modules, .git, build output and .env files.

healthcheck.title: Health check
healthcheck.fix: Add a HEALTHCHECK to the Dockerfile (or healthcheck in compose) so broken containers are noticed.

pinned.title: Base images without a fixed version: {{metric}}
pinned.fix: Pin the listed base images to a specific version instead of :latest or no tag.

envTracked.title: .env files kept out of git
envTracked.fix: Remove the listed .env files from git (git rm --cached), add .env to .gitignore, and change every secret that was in them.

secrets.title: Keys or passwords in the code: {{metric}}
secrets.fix: Move the secrets found in the listed lines to environment variables, and change (rotate) those keys, since they were committed.

publicKeys.title: Public client keys to restrict: {{metric}}
publicKeys.fix: These Google/Firebase client keys are public by design; make sure each one is restricted (app, website and API restrictions) in Google Cloud Console.

dangerous.title: Risky code patterns: {{metric}}
dangerous.fix: Review the listed eval, innerHTML, shell commands built from strings and similar: replace them with safe alternatives or sanitize the input.

exists.title: Tests: {{metric}} files
exists.fix: Add tests for the most important behaviour, starting with the code that breaks most often.

ratio.title: Test files per code file: {{metric}}
ratio.fix: Add tests for the main modules that have none yet (aim for about one test file per three code files).

script.title: One command runs the tests
script.fix: Add a "test" script (or pytest config) so the whole suite runs with one command.

ci.title: CI runs the tests
ci.fix: Make the CI workflow run the test suite, not just the build.

assets.title: Heavy files in the repo: {{metric}}
assets.fix: Compress or resize the listed assets (WebP/AVIF for images), or load them from a CDN.

lazy.title: Pages load only what they need
lazy.fix: Load rarely used pages and heavy components on demand (React.lazy / dynamic import).

readme.title: README length: {{metric}} characters
readme.fix: Expand the README: what the project does, how to install and run it, and how it's organised.

install.title: README explains how to start
install.fix: Add an "Install" and "Usage" section to the README with the exact commands.

license.title: License
license.fix: Add a LICENSE file so others know how they may use the code.

envExample.title: .env.example for settings
envExample.fix: Add a .env.example listing every environment variable the code reads, with empty or sample values.

any.title: Any documentation
any.fix: Add at least a README describing the project.

lockfile.title: Exact versions locked (lockfile)
lockfile.fix: Commit the lockfile so everyone installs the same versions.

loose.title: Unbounded versions: {{metric}}
loose.fix: Replace "*", "latest" and open-ended ">=" versions with normal ranges (for example ^1.2.3).

mixedLocks.title: One package manager
mixedLocks.fix: Keep a single package manager: remove the extra lockfiles in the listed folders.

deprecated.title: Deprecated packages: {{metric}}
deprecated.fix: Replace the listed deprecated packages with their maintained alternatives.

typecheck.title: Type check passes
typecheck.fix: Fix the type errors reported by the type check (see the output in "Run the project's own checks").

lint.title: Linter passes
lint.fix: Fix the problems the linter reports.

tests.title: Tests pass: {{metric}}
tests.fix: Make the failing tests pass, or fix the code they caught.

audit.title: Known vulnerabilities in dependencies: {{metric}}
audit.fix: Update the packages with known vulnerabilities (start with critical and high).

auditSecurity.title: Serious vulnerabilities in dependencies: {{metric}}
auditSecurity.fix: Update the packages with critical or high vulnerabilities now.

dead.title: Unused code: {{metric}}
dead.fix: Remove the unused files, exports and dependencies the project's dead-code tool lists, one at a time with the tests passing; or run the Safe cleanup team flow.

a11y.title: Accessibility problems on screen: {{metric}}
a11y.fix: Fix the accessibility problems the real-screen check found (missing labels, names and roles, keyboard traps), starting with the serious ones, on the pages listed.

contrast.title: Hard-to-read text on screen: {{metric}}
contrast.fix: Raise the contrast of the listed text to at least 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text), by changing the colors in the styles, not by hiding the text.

overflow.title: Pages wider than the screen: {{metric}}
overflow.fix: Make the listed pages fit the screen so nothing scrolls sideways (fixed widths, long words, wide tables or images), checking at phone width.

console.title: Errors in the browser: {{metric}}
console.fix: Fix the errors the browser logged on the listed pages.

images.title: Pictures that do not load: {{metric}}
images.fix: Fix the broken image addresses on the listed pages, or remove the pictures.

vitals.title: Slow or jumpy pages: {{metric}}
vitals.fix: Make the listed pages show their main content within 2.5 seconds and stop moving while they load (layout shift below 0.1): size images and placeholders, load less up front.

session.text: A conversation with an AI coding tool, from your first message to the last.

token.text: A small piece of text, about ¾ of a word. AI tools count what they read and write in tokens.

context.text: Everything the AI is keeping in mind right now. When it gets full, the AI starts forgetting earlier parts.

compaction.text: When the context is full, the tool shortens the conversation to keep going; details can get lost.

hub.text: A small server your team runs. It passes encrypted updates between you and can't read them.

e2e.text: Data is locked on your computer and only unlocked on your teammates' computers. Nobody in between can read it.

recoveryKey.text: A long code that unlocks your team's data if every device is lost. Keep it in a password manager.

twoFactor.text: Besides your password, a 6-digit code from an app on your phone.

commit.text: A saved snapshot of your code changes, with a short note about what changed.

branch.text: A separate line of work in Git, so changes don't touch the main code until you merge them.

push.text: Sending your saved changes (commits) to GitHub or another shared place.

deploy.text: Putting a new version of your app on the server where people use it.

staging.text: Staging is a test copy of your live app; Prod is the real one people use.

ssh.text: A secure way to run commands on another computer, such as your server.

env.text: A file with settings and secrets (passwords, keys) for your app. It must never be shared.

worktree.text: A second working copy of the same repo, so an agent can work without touching your files.

mcp.text: A standard way for AI tools to use other programs. Igrek offers one so Claude can read your project memory.

diff.text: The exact lines that were added or removed in a change.

blame.text: Shows, line by line, who last changed the code and when.

hook.text: A small script a tool runs at certain moments, for example when a session starts.

endpoint.text: One address of your API, like GET /users.

api.text: How programs talk to each other: one asks, the other answers with data.

ci.text: Checks that run automatically on every push, such as tests and lint.

rateLimit.text: How much you can use an AI tool in a time window (for example 5 hours or a week).

persona.text: An AI teammate with a role, such as "Security expert", with its own rules and focus.

persona.title: Expert team
persona.intro: Experts who have worked in their field all their life. Each keeps a notebook of its opinions and only changes its mind with new evidence. Talk to one, or ask several at once in a team meeting.
persona.scoreNote: Steps done and problems caught come from team runs (a review or gate that sent work back). Merged: share of its team runs you merged rather than threw away. Decisions kept: meetings whose decision went into project memory.
persona.exportBody: Writes each expert as a file your AI tools read on their own: Claude Code sub-agents (.claude/agents) in a project, or Codex custom prompts. Files are overwritten on the next export.
persona.exportCodex: Writes to the prompts folder of your Codex account; run one with /<expert id> in Codex.
persona.notebookEmpty: Nothing written down yet. Opinions appear here after chats and meetings.
persona.chatPick: In which project? The expert reads that project's memory and its own parts before it starts.
persona.f_idHint: a-z, 0-9 and dashes; used as the file name when exported
persona.f_web: May search and read the web (the chat then asks before every risky step)
persona.f_categories: Parts of the project it owns
persona.englishNote: The profile is written in English because the models follow it best. The expert always answers in your language.
persona.timelineHint: One per line: year — event. Only real, well-documented milestones.
persona.readingLibrary: Add the books you own: the expert then quotes them with the page.
persona.rulesHint: Extra rules for this expert only, one per line.
persona.rulesAll: Every expert also follows the expert rules: stay consistent with the notebook, change its mind only with new evidence, name sources, never invent numbers, rank by importance, give a confidence level.
persona.showPrompt: Show what it reads before it starts
persona.notebookHint: Claim, reasoning, evidence, confidence and date. A change needs new evidence; without it the old opinion stays.
persona.safetyNote: No expert pushes, merges, publishes or deploys on its own: those always wait for you.
persona.wizardTitle: Describe the expert in a sentence
persona.wizardBody: The AI drafts the whole profile: background, history of the field, reading list, checklist and traps. You check and change it before saving.
persona.wizardHint: For example: a payments expert who has run checkout for online shops in Europe for 15 years
persona.draftCheck: Check the draft, especially the years and books, then save.
persona.reviewTip: {{name}} looks at this part and reports what matters most
persona.reviewDraft: Review the {{section}} part of this project. Start with the open checks, then use your own checklist. List findings by importance with the file and line, say what to fix first, and give a confidence for each.

meeting.deciding: The team lead is weighing the answers…

testers.title: Test users
testers.intro: Ordinary people, not experts, try a task in your app in a real browser and think aloud while they do. Each runs in its own private browser, on its own device size, eyesight and connection. Use it only on your own app.
testers.noBrowser: Chromium or Google Chrome is needed on this computer for test users. Install it and reload this page. (The Docker image does not include a browser to stay small.)
testers.notLocal: This address is not on this computer or your local network. Test only apps you own; the test users act on whatever is there.
testers.task: What should they try to do?
testers.taskHint: For example: sign up and add your first product
testers.audienceHint: For example: Turkish mothers aged 25-35 living in Germany
testers.usageNote: Each test user is a Claude session with only browser tools: it cannot touch your files or run commands. Each one uses part of your Claude limit; at the same time means more speed and more load on this computer.
testers.auntHint: How easy it felt for people with little tech experience (0-100). Success: share who reached the goal.
testers.needProject: Pick a project for the test to send problems to an expert
testers.repeatTip: Same people, same task: did your change make it better?
testers.auto: Test again by itself after each new commit
testers.autoTip: When the project gets a new commit, the same people try the same task again and the result is compared with this one. At most once every two hours and never while another test runs, since each test uses model time. If it gets worse, you see it in the inbox.

library.title: Library
library.intro: What your experts read: books, documents, articles, web pages and GitHub repositories. They search it before answering and cite the page or chapter. Everything stays on this computer.
library.modelBody: Searching works by words right away. To find passages by meaning, in any language (a Turkish question finding an English book), Igrek uses a small model that runs on this computer. It is downloaded once ({{mb}} MB, free) from Hugging Face.
library.drop: Drop PDF, EPUB, Markdown, text or HTML files here
library.urlHint: A web page, an X post or a GitHub repository address
library.searchHint: Try a question, as an expert would ask it
library.empty: Nothing yet. Add a book you own, a document or a page; experts will cite it.
library.suggestHint: Free sources picked for your projects and your experts. Adding one downloads the page here, so experts can quote it, even offline.
library.suggestDocs: Docs of what your projects use
library.suggestDocsHint: Found in your projects' package files: official documentation for each.
library.suggestRefsHint: The standards and guides each expert works from (OWASP, WCAG, web.dev, Google SRE and more).
library.suggestBooks_one: {{count}} book your experts recommend is not here
library.suggestBooks_other: {{count}} books your experts recommend are not here
library.suggestBooksHint: Books are not free to download; if you own one, add its file and the expert will quote it with page numbers.

lessons.intro: Every mistake is written down once: a failed test or build, a change that was reverted, a checkpoint you went back to, an answer you called wrong. Before similar work, the matching lessons are put in front of the AI so the same mistake isn't made twice.
lessons.empty: No lessons yet. They appear here when something goes wrong and gets fixed.
lessons.title: Lesson
lessons.preventHint: What to do next time, e.g. run the migration on a copy first
lessons.ruleHint: This keeps coming back: make it a rule?
lessons.retroTip: Experts look back on this project: what went well, what went wrong, what we learned. It goes into the library.
lessons.retroDone: The retrospective is in the library.

knowledge.intro: Each expert reads the free, public sources of its field (Hacker News, Reddit, Lobsters, Mastodon, Bluesky, arXiv, GitHub, Product Hunt, blogs). The same story from several places is merged, rated from the expert's angle (important? real or hype? does it touch your projects?), and what matters goes into its library with the date and link.
knowledge.needsAi: background AI is off in Settings, so the schedule waits
knowledge.trendHint: Mentions in the stories read this week / the weekly average of the four weeks before.
knowledge.empty: Nothing read yet. Press Read the news now, or wait for the schedule.
knowledge.compare: Compare packages (npm names, for example react, svelte)
knowledge.compareSources: Numbers from the npm registry and download API, GitHub and the Hacker News search, fetched just now.
knowledge.sourcesHint: Comma-separated. Nothing here needs an account.
knowledge.src_feeds: RSS or Atom feeds (blogs, changelogs, newsletters, podcasts)
knowledge.xNote: X has no free legal way to read it automatically: paste the link of an important post into the Library instead.

board.requestHint: For example: add user login with e-mail and password
board.safety: The team works in its own copy of the repo, on its own branch, without asking. Nothing reaches your branch until you approve, and nothing is ever pushed.
board.archonOn: Archon is installed: its workflows are in the list too (ones that push or open pull requests are refused).
board.hint: Drag a card to Doing (or press its arrow) and the team starts. When the work is ready the card moves to Review; merging it moves it to Done.

flows.raiseWorking: Working. After this round Igrek scores the copy again.
flows.raiseNone: The copy was not measured: it changed nothing, or the scan could not run.
flows.raiseOpen_one: {{count}} finding is still open after the last round. Send it back with a note, or merge what improved.
flows.raiseOpen_other: {{count}} findings are still open after the last round. Send it back with a note, or merge what improved.
flows.raiseAll: Every finding of this part passes on the copy. The screen check counts again after you merge.
flows.title: Team run
flows.desc_feature: Plan and design (waits for your OK), backend and frontend side by side, build and tests, QA, security and DevOps review, one summary.
flows.desc_fix: Find and fix, build and tests, QA confirms.
flows.feedbackHint: What to change (needed when you send it back)
flows.readyTitle: The team is done: look and approve
flows.reviseHint: Something to change? Write it and send it back; the developers work again and the checks run again.
flows.mergeNote: Merging happens on this computer only. Pushing is up to you.
flows.mergedNote: Merged into {{branch}} on this computer. Push when you're ready.
flows.desc_task: One AI step does the job; if code changed, the checks must pass.
flows.desc_check: Build and tests, and a security review.
flows.desc_deps: Patch and minor updates, tests run; majors only listed.
flows.desc_spec: Requirements, design, then tasks with acceptance criteria are written into docs/specs and wait for your OK; only then the team codes, and QA checks every acceptance criterion.
flows.waitingLimit: The AI plan's limit is full. Nothing is lost: the team goes on by itself at {{time}}, when the limit resets. Igrek never switches accounts on its own.
flows.name_careful: Careful change (explore, plan, critique, work, review)
flows.name_cleanup: Safe cleanup (dead code, checks before and after)
flows.desc_cleanup: The checks must pass first; dead code is listed with evidence, you pick what goes, it is removed in a copy with one commit per removal, the same checks pass again and QA confirms nothing changed for users.
flows.blast_one: {{count}} file uses what changed ({{tests}} tests among them): worth checking before you merge
flows.blast_other: {{count}} files use what changed ({{tests}} tests among them): worth checking before you merge

schedules.title: Scheduled work
schedules.intro: Write what should happen and when, in a sentence. Igrek turns it into a schedule you confirm. At its time it runs as a team flow in its own copy of the repo, within its time and step limits; the result waits on its run page and changes need your OK.
schedules.sentenceHint: For example: every Friday morning update the dependencies
schedules.tplReq_nightly-check: Run the build and tests, and check the code for security problems.
schedules.tplReq_weekly-deps: Update the dependencies (patch and minor) and run the tests.
schedules.tplReq_daily-report: Report what changed yesterday and what needs attention.
schedules.tpl_down-check: Find out why the site is down
schedules.tplReq_ci-fix: CI failed. Find the cause in the failing run's log and fix it; the tests must pass.
schedules.tplReq_issue-triage: A new issue was opened. Say whether it is a real problem, where in the code it is, and what fixing it would take. Change nothing.
schedules.tplReq_down-check: The site is down. Find out why from the logs and the last changes, and say what to do. Change nothing.
schedules.on_app-error: when the app reports an error
schedules.safety: Runs never push or deploy. Times missed while this computer was off are not run on their own: you are asked.
schedules.confirm: Is this right? Nothing runs before you approve.
schedules.missed: It should have run at {{at}}, while this computer was off.
schedules.held_changed: It changed after you approved it, so it waits for your OK again before it runs.
schedules.held_expired: Your approval is over 90 days old; give your OK again to keep it running.

secrets.guardTip: Adds a pre-commit hook to this repo (in .git/hooks, not committed) that stops a commit adding a secret. Without Igrek running it lets commits through.

deps.hint: Compares each package with its newest version and looks up known vulnerabilities on OSV.dev. Checked once a day on its own.

templates.name: Name (letters, numbers, dashes)

backup.hint: One file with project memory, the lessons book, the library's texts, experts and their notebooks, schedules and ideas. Accounts, keys and .env backups are never in it. Restoring only adds what is missing.
backup.importPassword: Password of the file, if it has one

update.title: Updates
update.hint: Igrek checks its own git repository every 6 hours with your git login. Updating pulls, installs and builds; then it restarts.
update.dirty: Igrek's folder has local changes; commit or put them aside before updating.
update.failed: The update stopped; see the log.
update.docker: Running in Docker: update with git pull, then docker compose up -d --build.
update.none: This copy of Igrek is not a git checkout, so it can't update itself.

uptime.intro: Igrek opens these addresses on their own schedule from this computer. Two failed checks in a row count as down; you get an inbox item and a desktop notification.
uptime.emptyBody: Add the address of a site or API and Igrek tells you when it stops answering.

domains.intro: Once a day: the certificate on port 443, the domain's expiry from RDAP (the official successor of WHOIS) and the DNS records. Warnings come 30, 14, 7 and 1 days before anything runs out.
domains.emptyBody: Add a domain to be warned before its certificate or registration runs out.

docker.intro: Containers, their logs and resource use. Restarting, stopping and starting ask once; on a server they are written to the audit log.
docker.confirm_restart: Restart {{name}}? It is unavailable for a few seconds.
docker.confirm_stop: Stop {{name}}? Whatever it serves stops answering.

logs.noSources: No log sources yet. Add one below.
logs.noGroups: No errors or warnings in these lines.
logs.fixTip: The team finds the cause in its own copy of the project and fixes it; you approve before anything is merged.
logs.fixPick: Pick the project to fix it in first
logs.emptyBody: Add a log file, a container or a service, then read them all at once.

apperrors.title: Errors from your app

apperrors.setupNote: Set release to the commit of the build to see which commits an error started after. Without it, Igrek uses the commit the project is on. Apps on another computer can't reach Igrek's local address.
apperrors.noSuspects: No commit range known yet: send a release with each build.
apperrors.emptyBody: Connect the app with a few lines of code; errors are grouped here and each knows the commit it started with.

diagram.error: The diagram could not be drawn

db.intro: SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL and MongoDB: tables, rows, the schema as a diagram and a query editor. Addresses are stored encrypted on this computer and never sent to AI.
db.found: Found in the project (the value is not shown):
db.name: Name (optional)
db.prodHint: Production databases are read-only: queries run inside a read-only transaction.
db.privacy: The address and password stay encrypted on this computer. Query results are never sent to AI; asking the expert sends the query, the schema and the plan only.
db.addedButFailed: Saved, but it could not connect: {{error}}
db.readOnlyTip: Queries can't change anything. Click to allow writes.
db.writableTip: Writes are allowed after a confirmation. Click to make it read-only.
db.unlock: Allow queries that change data? Each one still asks first.
db.unlockProd: This is production. Allowing writes means a wrong query can damage live data. Each write still asks first.
db.askTip: Sends the query, the schema of the tables it uses and the query plan; never any rows.
db.confirmWrite: This query changes data. Run it?
db.readOnlyRefused: This database is read-only, so the query was not run. Allow writes in its settings first.
db.truncated: more rows exist; showing the first 500
db.emptyBody: Add a database by address, or pick one Igrek found in a project's .env or folder.
db.healthHint: Looks for problems in the data with read-only queries: rows pointing at rows that do not exist, values repeated where they should be unique (email, slug), NULLs in columns that are almost always filled, negative prices or quantities, and the same value written in different ways (case, spaces, accents).
db.healthProd: This is a production database. The scan only reads, but confirm before it runs.
db.healthClean: No problems found in the data.
db.anomalyVariants_one: {{count}} value written more than one way
db.anomalyVariants_other: {{count}} values written more than one way

backups.intro: Database and folder backups on a schedule. Each new backup is tested: restored into a temporary database or a copy and counted, so a broken backup is found before you need it.
backups.name: Name

perf.cacheTitle: Cache and compression of the live site
perf.cacheHint: Fetches the page and the scripts and styles it loads once, and checks their headers: the page must not stay cached after a deploy, hashed files should be cached for a year, text files should come compressed, and changeable files need a validator.
perf.cacheClean: Nothing to fix in the headers.
perf.cache_htmlCachedLong: The page stays cached for long
perf.cacheFix_htmlCachedLong: Send the HTML with Cache-Control: no-cache (and an ETag), so a new deploy is seen at once; long caching belongs to hashed files.
perf.cache_hashedNotImmutable: A hashed file is not cached for long
perf.cacheFix_hashedNotImmutable: Its name changes with its content, so it can be cached for good: Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable.
perf.cacheFix_noValidator: Add an ETag or Last-Modified header so a browser can check for a newer version without downloading it again.
perf.cacheFix_notCompressed: Turn on brotli or gzip for text files (HTML, JS, CSS, JSON, SVG) in the server or the CDN; they usually shrink to a third.
perf.cacheFix_noCache: Give it a Cache-Control header, and put a content hash in its name so it can be cached for a year.
perf.renderHint: Read from the code (Next.js): SSG is built once, ISR is rebuilt on a timer, SSR renders on every request, CSR fetches in the browser. A suggestion appears when the page's data fits another one better.
perf.render_browserFetchPublic: The page fetches its data in the browser after it loads, though nothing in it is personal: fetch it in a server component so it is in the first HTML (faster first paint, visible to search engines).
perf.render_dynamicNotPersonal: It renders on every request (no-store) but shows the same thing to everyone: cache it and refresh on a timer (export const revalidate = 60) or when the data changes (revalidateTag).
perf.render_serverPropsPublic: getServerSideProps runs on every request though the page is the same for everyone: use getStaticProps with revalidate.
perf.render_streamWithLoading: It renders per request for the signed-in user; add a loading.tsx so the shell shows at once and the data streams in.
perf.render_preRenderParams: A page with a URL parameter that fetches data but lists no generateStaticParams: known pages are built on first visit only; list the common ones to build them ahead.
perf.render_staticDataGoesStale: It fetches data at build time and never refreshes: add a revalidate time, or it shows build-day data until the next deploy.
perf.codeCacheClean: Every cache found sets an expiry.
perf.codeCache_redisNoExpiry: A Redis value is set without an expiry (EX/PX): it stays until someone deletes it, even after the data changed.
perf.codeCache_lruNoTtl: An LRU cache without a ttl: entries only leave when it is full, so old data can be served for a long time.
perf.codeCache_nodeCacheNoTtl: node-cache without stdTTL: entries never expire.
perf.codeCache_unstableCacheNoRevalidate: unstable_cache without revalidate: the result is kept until a deploy or a revalidateTag call.
perf.codeCache_noInvalidation: The code caches values but never deletes or refreshes a key: after data changes, readers may see the old value until it expires (or forever).

arch.title: Architecture pattern
arch.about_layered: Presentation, business and data in their own layers. Its rule: a request goes down one layer at a time (closed layers), so the screens never reach the database directly and no layer reaches up.
arch.about_eventDriven: Parts talk through a message broker or queue instead of calling each other: they can scale and change separately, but a flow is harder to follow and test.
arch.about_microkernel: A small core with plug-ins: features are added as plug-ins without touching the core.
arch.about_microservices: Separately deployed services, each with its own code and image: fast to change and scale one by one, slower when a request crosses many services.
arch.about_unknown: No folders that name layers, no message broker, no plug-ins and no separate services were found. Most small projects are a simple monolith; that is fine while they stay small.
arch.source: Patterns and ratings: Mark Richards, Software Architecture Patterns (O'Reilly, 2015).
arch.needsHint: Pick what matters most for this project:
arch.misfit: This pattern is weak on {{qualities}}, which you marked as important. Weigh a change of pattern for the parts where it matters, with the architect expert.
arch.fit: The pattern rates high on everything you marked as important.
arch.ask_background: Long jobs or work that reacts to events (emails, imports, payments)
arch.ask_plugins: Others will add features as plug-ins
arch.why_plugins: Features as plug-ins need a small, stable core: the microkernel pattern.
arch.why_largeTeam: Several teams can then work and release on their own.
arch.why_highScale: Each service scales by itself under high load.
arch.why_dailyReleases: Small services can be released many times a day without touching the rest.
arch.why_background: Long or reactive work goes through a queue instead of blocking requests.
arch.why_scaleParts: The busy parts can be scaled separately.
arch.why_smallTeam: For a small team a layered, modular monolith is the easiest to build and test.
arch.why_modules: A modular monolith with clear modules lets teams split parts out later.
arch.why_queueLater: Start background jobs with a simple queue inside the app; split it out only when it grows.
arch.why_startSimple: Distribution has a cost; pay for it when the team or the load asks for it.
arch.newNote: The decision is written to docs/adr/0001-architecture.md with its rules, a C4 skeleton goes to docs/architecture.md, and the rules go into AGENTS.md so every AI follows them.

design.title: Design patterns and SOLID
design.clean: Nothing stands out: no Singleton sprawl, lonely interfaces, long type switches or SOLID breaks were found.
design.fix_singleton: A Singleton is global state with a pattern's name: it hides dependencies and makes tests share state. Pass the object in where it is needed.
design.fix_singleImplementation: An abstraction nothing else uses yet (speculative generality). Keep the class alone until a second implementation (or a test double) needs the interface.
design.rule_bigSwitch: A long switch on a type
design.fix_bigSwitch: Each new case means editing this switch (and its copies). A map of handlers, or the Strategy or State pattern, puts each case in one place.
design.rule_refusedBequest: A subclass refuses what it inherits
design.fix_refusedBequest: A method that throws 'not implemented' breaks the Liskov principle: code using the parent breaks on this child. Use composition, or split the parent's interface.
design.rule_godClass: A class that does too much
design.fix_godClass: Very long classes have more than one reason to change (single responsibility). Extract the separate jobs into their own classes.
design.fix_hardDependency: Creating its own services with new ties the class to them (dependency inversion): pass them in through the constructor so they can be swapped and tested.

experts.intro: Each expert looks at this project from its own field: the architect at how it is built, UI/UX at the screens, security at the risks. They only read the code. A look is one model call; chats also ask them when a question needs one.
experts.noView: {{name}} has not looked at this project yet.

experts.askAllTip: The core experts who have not looked yet read the project, three at a time

move.title: Move to another computer
move.hint: Everything Igrek keeps (projects, chats' history, memory, library, experts, settings) in one file locked with a password. Open it in Igrek on the other computer and restart; the folder it replaces is kept. AI logins are not in it: log in again there. Projects whose folders sit elsewhere on the new computer are added again on the Projects page.
move.password: Password for the file (at least 8 characters)
move.passwordRule: The file holds your database and keys, so it is always locked: choose a password of at least 8 characters, and use the same one to open it.
move.saved: Move file downloaded. Copy it to the other computer and open it there.
move.waiting: The moved-in data is ready; it takes over when Igrek restarts.

chatTodos.placeholder: Add something to do, then Enter
chatTodos.useTip: Puts what is left into the box; you send it.
chatTodos.handOver: These are still left in this chat's list:

install.title: Igrek as an app
install.hint: Opens in a window of its own, with no tabs or address bar, and gets a place in the start menu or the dock. It is still the same Igrek on this computer; nothing new is downloaded.
install.done: Igrek is running as an app.
install.manual: Your browser does not offer it from here. In Chrome or Edge use the install icon at the end of the address bar (or the menu: Cast, save and share > Install page as app); Safari: File > Add to Dock.

desktop.autostartHint: Igrek opens by itself when you sign in to your computer. Off until you turn it on.
desktop.updateHint: The app downloads the new version, checks that Igrek signed it with its own key, and restarts.
desktop.updateOff: This copy of the app was built without an update key, so it cannot update itself. Download the new version from the Releases page.
desktop.updateNotice: Igrek {{version}} is ready. Install it in Settings > Updates.
desktop.preparing: Getting Igrek ready for its first start: {{mb}} of about 35 MB downloaded

packs.catalogHint: Packages Igrek has reviewed, read from Igrek's GitHub page when you ask.
packs.catalogEmpty: The catalog is empty for now.
packs.openOwn: Open a package of your own
packs.notJson: That file is not a package.

packs.name: Package name
packs.nothingToShare: You have no experts of your own yet; make one on the Team tab, then share it here.

screen.title: The real screen
screen.hint: Opens the running app in a browser at laptop and phone width and measures what a person meets: accessibility, contrast, pages wider than the screen, errors, broken pictures and loading. No model is called.
screen.last: Last checked {{when}}. The pictures show the time before next to now.
screen.checkTip: Opens the app's home page and a few pages it links to; takes about a minute.
screen.needPreview: The check opens the running app, so the live preview must be running.
screen.overflow: Wider than the screen: it scrolls sideways

private.title: My private details
private.hint: Write details like your ID number, student number, IBAN, passwords or your company's figures here. They stay locked on this computer. The AI never sees them: it only gets a nickname in their place. The real value is put back only on your computer, when it is needed (in a step you approve, in an answer you copy, in a form the browser extension fills).
private.label: What it is (for example T.C. kimlik)
private.name: Short name
private.nameTip: The AI sees this detail only under this nickname. Use lowercase letters, digits and _.
private.removeConfirm: Remove "{{label}}"? Chats will no longer hide it.
private.guard: This message seems to hold a {{what}} that is not among your private details. Hide it, and the AI sees only a nickname, not the real value.
private.hiddenTip: Hidden: the AI saw a nickname in its place. The real value stays on this computer.
private.guardOnceTip: Not saved: hidden in this chat or quick question only. Its answers show the real value while it is open; after Igrek restarts they keep the placeholder.
private.copyTip: Copies the answer with your real values in place of the placeholders. The AI never saw them.
private.inStep: Igrek puts your real private details in place of the placeholders when this step runs; the AI does not see them. If the step prints a value, its output can reach the AI.
private.gatewayOn: On: wherever the AI looks (your messages, files it reads, the results of commands it runs), these details and the secret keys in your projects are replaced by their nicknames. This works for Claude and Codex. The AI can never open your secret key files.
private.gatewayOff: Off: only what you type in a chat is hidden; files the AI reads and command results go as they are.
private.gatewayStats: Details protected: {{values}}. Hidden from the AI so far: {{hidden}} times.
private.filesHint: Like your .env files: in Igrek's chats with Claude, the AI cannot read these, in any project. A name or pattern counts in every folder (bordro*.pdf, finans/*.xlsx); a full path only there. A command that prints one still goes through the privacy gateway, which hides only your saved details.
private.filesBrackets: A file pattern may not hold brackets.

extension.title: Browser extension
extension.hint: For forms in your browser (job and scholarship applications, company paperwork): it fills the fields that ask for your private details and has a field's text written, and the AI never sees those details. It talks only to Igrek on this computer.
extension.step1: In Chrome, Brave or Edge open the extensions page (chrome://extensions), turn on Developer mode and choose Load unpacked.
extension.step2: Pick the extension folder inside Igrek's folder.
extension.step3: In the extension's panel press "Connect" and allow it here when Igrek asks (or make a pairing key below and paste it).
extension.forgetConfirm: Disconnect every paired browser? Each needs a new key afterwards.
extension.keyOnce: Shown only now. It lets the extension read your private details on this computer, so paste it only into your own browser.
extension.pairAsk: The browser extension asks to connect
extension.pairBody: Allow it only if the extension shows this same code. It can then fill forms with your private details on this computer and act on pages with your OK.

phone.usb2: Settings, Developer options: turn on USB debugging, and plug the phone into this computer.
phone.usb3: Allow this computer on the phone when it asks, then press Refresh above.
phone.wifiHint: Developer options, Wireless debugging, Pair device with pairing code: write the address and code it shows, press Pair, then write the address on the Wireless debugging page and press Connect.
phone.unauthorized: Allow this computer on the phone (a question is waiting on its screen), then press Refresh.
phone.screen: The phone's screen; click to tap
phone.noScreen: The screen could not be read; is the phone unlocked?
phone.typeHint: Text to type on the phone
phone.noApk: No built APK in this project yet. Build it (for example ./gradlew assembleDebug, flutter build apk or npx react-native build-android), then choose it again.
phone.checkHint: Reads what is on the phone's screen now: buttons too small for a finger (under 48 dp), buttons a screen reader cannot name, and the crashes the phone logged.
phone.unnamed_one: {{count}} button has no name for a screen reader
phone.unnamed_other: {{count}} buttons have no name for a screen reader

coding.title: Do you write code?
coding.body: Igrek shows what fits you. Nothing is taken away: you can switch any time in Settings.
coding.noBody: Simple: a project shows its overview, chats and files, in plain words.
coding.yesBody: Developer: code, board, health, setup and tools too, with the usual terms (branch, commit).

projects.aheadTip: Saved changes not sent online yet
projects.behindTip: Changes in the online copy you do not have yet

inbox.notice_secret: A password or key was saved into the project's history

setup.hooksBody: Adds a small automatic step to this project's local Claude Code settings. Every new chat then starts with the memory above. Your project is not changed: the file stays out of its history.

term.forkHint: Starts a new version of this conversation; the original stays as it is.

enhance.ctxTip_git: Which line of work, changes not saved yet and the last saved changes. Click to leave it out.

copy.banner: Working in a separate copy ({{branch}}, made from {{base}}). Your folder isn't touched until you bring the changes in.
copy.mergeTip: Bring these changes into your folder. Nothing is sent online.
copy.mergeConfirm: Bring the changes from this copy into your folder ({{branch}})? Nothing is sent online.
copy.merged: Brought into your folder ({{branch}}). Sending it online is up to you.
copy.discardConfirm: Stop this chat and delete its copy? Changes you didn't bring in are lost.

board.safety: The team works in its own copy of the project, without asking. Nothing reaches your folder until you approve, and nothing is ever sent online.

update.dirty: Igrek's folder has changes of its own; save or put them aside before updating.

trust.title: The project's own automatic steps and connected tools
trust.hint: A project can bring automatic steps and connected tools that run commands. Chats use them only after you trust them, and ask again when they change.

help.d_settings: Language, theme, a free local model through Ollama, your own connected tools, notifications to Telegram, Discord or e-mail, backups, updates, disk and network.

settings.aiMay_ship: Sending your work online, putting it live or publishing it always waits for your OK.

chat.modeHint_auto: Claude decides what's safe and runs it, in a separate copy of your project. Sending online, bringing changes in and putting it live still always ask.
chat.guard_ship: This would send your work out (online, live or published). AI never does that on its own, so it asks every time.

start.label: What do you want to do?
start.placeholder: What do you want to do? Igrek takes it to the right project: "Add a cart page to the shop"
start.placeholderProject: What do you want to do in this project?
start.whereTip: Igrek picks: the chief, who knows every project, hands it to the right one. Or pick the project yourself.
start.historyEmpty: What you start from the "What do you want to do?" box shows here.
start.manyPick: Each picked project works on it in its own copy
start.manyNote_one: {{count}} project: one run, in its own copy. Nothing reaches your folders until you approve each one.
start.manyNote_other: {{count}} projects: one run each, in its own copy, and each uses your Claude limit. Nothing reaches your folders until you approve each one.
start.playbook_bug: Sent with the bug-fix steps: reproduce first, root cause, smallest fix.
start.playbook_perf: Sent with the speed steps: measure before, one change at a time, measure after.
start.playbook_refactor: Sent with the restructuring steps: the behaviour stays the same, tests before and after.
start.playbook_feature: Sent with the new-feature steps: the data first, the smallest version, tests.
start.playbookTip: Igrek recognised the kind of task and adds a way of working: the AI first says the goal back, follows the steps, and ends with the decisions it made.

fix.tip: Igrek shows the command first and runs it only when you say so. No AI model is used.
fix.title: Run this command?
fix.body: It runs in a terminal here, so you see everything it prints and can stop it.

batch.title: One task, several projects
batch.emptyBody: Pick "Several projects" in the "What do you want to do?" box to send one task to several projects.
batch.hint: Open a project's run to read its changes and merge them, or not. Each is decided on its own.

agentFiles.title: One memory for Claude and Codex
agentFiles.claudeOnly: The project's rules are in CLAUDE.md, which only Claude Code reads. Codex and other agents read AGENTS.md, so they do not know them.
agentFiles.apart_one: CLAUDE.md (Claude Code) and AGENTS.md (Codex and others) differ in {{count}} rule: one agent knows it, the other does not.
agentFiles.apart_other: CLAUDE.md (Claude Code) and AGENTS.md (Codex and others) differ in {{count}} rules: one agent knows them, the other does not.
agentFiles.joinTip: Every rule goes into AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md just brings it in (@AGENTS.md), so both agents read the same rules. A snapshot is taken first. No AI model is used.
agentFiles.joined: Claude and Codex read the same rules (CLAUDE.md brings in AGENTS.md).

handoff.viaTeam: Send to my other computers and the team
handoff.viaTeamHint: Through your team hub, encrypted. It waits on the Projects page there.
handoff.viaFileHint: Carry it over yourself and open it on the Projects page there.
handoff.sent: Sent. It waits on the Projects page of your other computers.
handoff.saved: Saved. Open it on the other computer's Projects page.
handoff.waiting: Chats to go on with here
handoff.stashAndContinue: Put my changes aside and go on
handoff.openTip: A chat saved on another computer with "Go on elsewhere".
handoff.badFile: That is not a hand-off file.
handoff.problem_not-git: The project is not a git repository here, so the code cannot be brought to the same state.
handoff.problem_not-shared: This project is not shared with your team hub. Turn sharing on in its Setup, or save the chat as a file.
handoff.problem_dirty: This computer has unsaved changes in the project. Igrek can put them aside (git stash) so nothing is lost; git stash pop brings them back.
handoff.problem_missing-commit: The commit this chat was on could not be found here, even after fetching. Push it on the other computer, then try again.
handoff.problem_apply-failed: The changes could not be applied; nothing of yours was overwritten.
handoff.problem_file-exists: A new file from the other computer already exists here with different content.
